mainEntity.name: Why do "billion" mean different things in different countries?

acceptedAnswer.text: The US and modern UK use the "short scale," where each new name is 1000× the last (million, billion = 10⁹, trillion = 10¹²). Much of continental Europe traditionally uses the "long scale," where billion = 10¹² and milliard fills the 10⁹ spot — this calculator supports both.

mainEntity.name: Why do checks write out amounts in words?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under the Uniform Commercial Code and similar laws elsewhere, if the written words and the numeric figure on a check disagree, the words legally control — a safeguard against a single altered digit changing the amount.

mainEntity.name: How are cents handled on a check?

acceptedAnswer.text: Conventionally written as a fraction over 100, e.g. "and 75/100 Dollars," rather than spelled out — reducing ambiguity, since the fraction format is instantly recognizable.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between a cardinal and an ordinal number?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cardinal numbers count quantity (one, two, three); ordinal numbers describe position or rank (first, second, third). Only the final word of a spelled-out number changes form for the ordinal — "twenty-three" becomes "twenty-third."

mainEntity.name: Is there a limit to how large a number this can spell out?

acceptedAnswer.text: Named scale words are supported up to the short-scale decillion (10³³) / long-scale equivalent; beyond that, the number is shown in scientific notation instead, since no widely agreed English name exists.
